newsitem.title: USA: Using corporate imagination to create workplace benefits.
newsitem.headline: Using corporate imagination to create workplace benefits.

text.p: Starbucks Corp. is one example of a work place where the company's "social vision" -- what one author calls "moral imagination" -- pays benefits for employees and also helps the employer.
David Hudson, a 19-year-old college business student, might consider himself well off just to earn $7.21 an hour at a part-time service job at the company's Gaithersburg, Md., coffee bar.
But Starbucks also provides a health plan and, best of all, "Bean Stock" that allows him to invest about 10 percent of his paycheck in options on Starbucks stock.
"They pay us well and expect us to work up to their standards," said Hudson, who has worked in the cafe since May of last year.

To earn "Bean Stock," Hudson must put in at least 20 hours weekly between April 1st and Sept. 30th, the end of Starbucks' fiscal year, and remain employed until stock is distributed the following January.
Hudson buys his option to purchase future stock at a fixed price. If the shares rise in value, so will his potential profits.
Over 10 years, a Starbucks "partner" can amass stock options equalling three times his or her salary, noted Corey Rosen, director of the Centre for Employee Ownership, in Oakland, Calif.

In addition, partners pay a fourth of their health insurance premium and get a 25-cent donation from Starbucks for each dollar they invest in their 401(k) retirement plan. Even part-timers get paid vacations and personal days off.
Seattle-based Starbucks is a prototype of firms whose owners have got what business author David Bollier calls "moral imagination."
They "integrate their own moral and personal values with their business lives and use them as a business strategy," he said.

"Employees with as little as six months of service can participate" in the options plan," Bollier noted. "But the longer one stays with the company, the more options granted and, potentially, the more valuable they become."

He praises 25 such firms in his new book, "Aiming Higher" (Amacom), and ranks Starbucks up there with savvy employers Merck, Inland Steel, GE Plastics, Xerox, and Levi Strauss. Each won a "social vision" award for their employee compensation plans from the Business Enterprise Trust, the nonprofit organisation of Hollywood producer Norman Lear.
Starbucks' growth began in 1982, when Howard Schultz was brought in as marketing chief by its founders, three college professors who named their firm after the first mate in "Moby Dick."
"Starbucks was not doing anything but selling coffee by the pound," Schultz said. "I thought (opening coffee bars) was an untapped opportunity for us."
On a buying trip to Italy, he discovered that Milan had 1,500 coffee bars, where, Schultz recalled, customers imbibed "a feeling of safety, of warmth, of comfort" along with their brew.
In 1987, Schultz and his backers bought Starbucks for $4 million and began growing their beans into a coffee bar chain.
To lure and retain dedicated workers, Schultz created a benefits package that he claims, is "the single greatest advantage we have in our company in terms of a competitive advantage."
That was critical, as many speciality retailers suffer from turnover rates as high as 300 percent a year.
Paying insurance premiums costs, but Schultz claims that the company's turnover rate -- under 60 percent -- means it comes out ahead, beginning with reduced training bills.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
